title: Choosing an Electrical EPC Contractor: A Buyer's Checklist
excerpt: Ten questions to ask before you award an electrical package for a data centre, plant or large building, and the evidence a good contractor should be able to show you.
content:
The electrical package is rarely the largest line in a project budget, but it is the one that decides whether the facility can be energised on the day it is meant to open. A late or faulty electrical handover holds up commissioning, occupancy and revenue.

These are the questions we would ask if we were on the buyer's side of the table.

Have they delivered this kind of facility before

Ask for projects of a similar type and size, not a long client list. A contractor who has energised a 45 MW data hall understands redundancy and commissioning levels. One who has delivered a chemical plant understands hazardous areas and process shutdowns. Ask for named projects, the scope they carried, and a reference you can call.

Can they show you client completion letters

Completion certificates from clients are the most reliable evidence available. They confirm that the work was finished, accepted, and usually say something about safety and quality. A contractor with a long track record should be able to share several.

What is their safety record, in numbers

Safety culture shows up in data. Ask for:

- Safe man-hours worked over the last few years

- Lost-time injuries (LTIs) over the same period

- A signed HSE policy from the top of the company

- How sub-contractor workers are inducted and supervised

A contractor who cannot give you numbers is probably not measuring them.

How do they control quality on site

Good quality control is a documented process, not a promise. Look for approved method statements before work starts, incoming material inspection against approved makes, stage-wise joint inspections, testing with calibrated instruments, and a formal way of closing non-conformances.

Who handles statutory approvals

High-voltage installations need approval from the Electrical Inspector (CEIG) before they can be energised. Confirm that the contractor has done this before in your state and that the approval is in their scope, not left as a gap between packages.

Can they support commissioning, not just installation

On data centres and critical facilities, testing and commissioning is where schedules are won or lost. Ask whether the contractor's engineers will stay through the commissioning levels and work with the commissioning agent until the facility is ready to serve.

Do they have the people and the balance sheet

Large packages need a deep bench of site engineers, supervisors and skilled workers, plus the working capital to buy material ahead of payment milestones. Ask about team size, revenue and how many sites they are running in parallel.

How do they work with your other contractors

Electrical work interfaces with civil, mechanical, fire and IT packages. Ask how they plan work fronts, attend coordination meetings and resolve clashes, and ask for an example of a multi-contractor site they have delivered.

What happens after handover

Confirm what documentation you will receive: as-built drawings, test reports, O&M manuals and warranties. Ask who your contact is if something fails in the defect liability period.

Are their prices clear

A very low bid often means scope has been left out. Compare bids against the same BOQ and ask each bidder to list their exclusions.

How EVIO answers these questions

Since 2011, EVIO has delivered turnkey electrical and automation projects for clients including Microsoft, NTT DATA, ST Telemedia, Flipkart, Yokohama and Tata Communications. Our project pages include the clients' own completion letters, and our company-wide safety record is more than 1.9 crore safe man-hours from FY21 to FY25 with zero lost-time injuries.

If you are preparing a tender, send us your drawings or BOQ and we will come back with a priced proposal and a list of exclusions.

title: How We Take a Data Centre's Electrical Systems from Installation to Ready to Serve
excerpt: Method statements, material inspection, joint inspections, calibrated testing and commissioning levels: the quality steps behind a reliable data hall.
content:
A data centre is sold on uptime. Every megawatt of IT load depends on HT and LT panels, transformers, UPS systems, DG sets, busduct and thousands of cable terminations working first time and every time after that.

Most failures that show up during commissioning, or worse after go-live, start as small things on site: a termination torqued incorrectly, a cable bent past its radius, a panel that does not match the approved make. Our quality process is designed to catch these early.

Approved method statements before work starts

Every work activity, from cable pulling to HT termination, has a method statement approved by the client before work begins. It defines the sequence, the tools, the checks and the safety controls. Site teams work to the method statement, not to memory.

Incoming material inspection

Material is checked when it arrives on site through an Incoming Material Inspection Report (IMIR). Each item is compared with the approved make, the specification and its test certificates. Anything that does not match is rejected before it can be installed.

Joint inspection at every stage

Before one stage of work is covered by the next, we raise a Request for Work Inspection (RFWI) and inspect jointly with the client's team. Cable trays are inspected before cables are pulled, and cables before they are dressed and terminated. Problems are cheap to fix at this point.

Testing with calibrated instruments

Installed systems are tested with calibrated instruments, and the results are recorded:

- Insulation resistance on cables and equipment

- Continuity of conductors and protective earth

- Earth resistance of the earthing network

- Torque on bolted connections and terminations

Commissioning levels L1 to L5

Data centre commissioning runs through levels, and every piece of equipment is tagged as it passes each one. It starts at L1, with installation verified, and ends at L5, when the systems have been tested together and the facility is ready to serve. Our engineers support the commissioning agent through every level.

Closing non-conformances properly

When something does go wrong, we do not just fix the symptom. Non-conformances are closed through root-cause analysis and corrective and preventive action (CAPA), so the same problem does not appear on the next floor or the next data hall.

The result

This process has been applied across data centre programmes for Microsoft, NTT DATA, Sify, CtrlS, AdaniConneX, Digital Edge and ST Telemedia, with about 295 MW of data centre capacity worked on across 10 Indian cities.

Planning a data hall or a campus expansion? Share your single-line diagram or BOQ and our data centre team will respond with a proposal.

title: CEIG Approval for HT Installations: What Plant Owners Should Plan For
excerpt: Why high-voltage installations need the Electrical Inspector's approval before energisation, and how to keep it from delaying your start-up.
content:
When a plant adds a new HT feeder, substation or transformer, the work is not finished when the last cable is terminated. Before the installation can be energised, it has to be inspected and approved by the Electrical Inspector, often called CEIG approval after the Chief Electrical Inspector to Government.

Why approval is needed

Under the Central Electricity Authority's safety regulations, high-voltage installations must be inspected before they are put into service. The inspector checks that the installation is safe and meets the regulations: clearances, earthing, protection, and that the equipment and test results are in order.

Without this approval the installation cannot legally be energised, so a missed approval delays production, however good the installation is.

What the inspector looks at

The details vary by state, but an inspection usually covers:

- Drawings and single-line diagrams of the installation

- Equipment ratings and test certificates

- Earthing and earth resistance values

- Protection settings and relay testing

- Clearances, barriers and safety signage

- Pre-commissioning test reports for cables, transformers and switchgear

How to avoid delays

Most approval delays are caused by missing or inconsistent documents, not by the installation itself. Plan for it from the start:

- Make the approval part of the electrical contractor's scope, so one party owns it

- Keep test reports and certificates organised as the work progresses

- Fix observations from internal inspections before the inspector visits

- Book the inspection early, as waiting times vary between states

An example

At Yokohama's Bahadurgarh plant, EVIO's scope for the Phase 3.0 expansion covered supply, installation and commissioning of the 6.6 kV downstream system, and the CEIG approval. Yokohama's completion letter confirms that the work was completed with zero accidents.

title: A Look at Execution Standards from Adani Connex, Pune
excerpt: Building Reliability Through Discipline: A Look at Execution Standards from Adani Connex, Pune
content:
Building Reliability Through Discipline: A Look at Execution Standards from Adani Connex, Pune

In high-dependency environments like data centers, electrical systems are expected to perform without failure – continuously, efficiently, and safely.

While design plays a crucial role, it is the quality of execution on site that ultimately determines how well a system performs over time. Small decisions like how cables are routed, how terminations are done, how materials are handled, can significantly influence long-term reliability.

Using examples from our recent data center project in Pune, this article highlights key electrical practices that contribute to building dependable infrastructure.

Cable Management: More Than Just Neatness

The way cables are routed; both vertically and horizontally, has a direct impact on system performance.

As seen in the picture vertical cable drops and horizontal dressing, structured routing with consistent spacing and alignment helps in:

- Simplifying maintenance and future modifications

- Reducing thermal buildup

- Ensuring clarity in complex installations

Well-managed cables are easier to inspect, troubleshoot, and scale.

Maintaining Proper Bending Radius

Cables are designed to operate within specific bending limits. Exceeding these limits can damage internal conductors and insulation.

The bending radius implementation seen in the picture demonstrates how controlled routing helps maintain these limits. This practice:

- Prevents mechanical stress

- Preserves cable life

- Ensures consistent electrical performance

It’s a detail that often goes unnoticed but has long-term implications.

Handling of HT Cables

High Tension cables require careful handling due to their load-bearing role in the system.

The single core HT cable dressing in the picture shows organized placement, appropriate spacing, and phase identification. Such practices help in:

- Minimizing interference between phases

- Improving safety and accessibility

- Supporting efficient heat dissipation

Cable Tray Installation: Structural Backbone

Cable trays are not just supports they define the routing discipline of the entire system.

The installations visible in the picture reflect well-aligned and properly supported trays, which contribute to:

- Load-bearing stability

- Clear segregation of different cable types

- Flexibility for future expansion

Proper tray installation ensures that the system remains adaptable over time.

Termination Quality Matters

Cable termination is a critical point in any electrical system. Even minor inconsistencies here can lead to failures.

The termination examples in the picture highlight clean connections, proper insulation, and clear identification. Good termination practices typically ensure:

- Reliable electrical contact

- Lower resistance and heat generation

- Easier inspection and maintenance

Earthing Systems: Safety at the Core

An effective earthing system is essential for both safety and equipment protection.

The earthing connections and earth bus system shown in the picture illustrate structured grounding practices with identifiable connections. This supports:

- Safe dissipation of fault currents

- Protection of sensitive equipment

- Traceability during inspections

Equipment Installation and Accessibility

Electrical panels and equipment need to be installed with both operation and maintenance in mind.

From the equipment installation layouts (page 9) , it is evident that spacing, alignment, and accessibility are key considerations. This enables:

- Safer operations

- Efficient monitoring

- Ease of servicing

Site Organization: Enabling Better Execution

Behind every well-executed project is a well-managed site.

The organized site store here reflects structured material handling and storage practices. Good site management contributes to:

- Reduced material damage and loss

- Improved workflow efficiency

- Enhanced safety conditions

In electrical projects, reliability is rarely the result of a single decision. It is built through a series of consistent, well-executed practices across every stage of installation.

From cable routing to earthing, from termination to site management, attention to detail plays a defining role in how systems perform over time.

Because in the end, good practices don’t just improve execution, they shape outcomes.

title: Mastering the Standards for Indoor and Outdoor Lighting
excerpt: Lighting today is no longer just about visibility—it’s about creating intelligent, sustainable, and human-centric spaces. At the heart of this evolution is the EN 12464 standard, which defines the…
content:
Lighting today is no longer just about visibility—it’s about creating intelligent, sustainable, and human-centric spaces. At the heart of this evolution is the EN 12464 standard, which defines the requirements for lighting workplaces to ensure visual comfort, safety, and occupant wellbeing.

At EVIO, we are committed to helping our clients implement smarter lighting strategies that align with these global benchmarks, ensuring every project is efficient, compliant, and future-ready.

The Core Focus: EN 12464-1 for Indoor Workplaces

The cornerstone of lighting design remains the EN 12464-1 standard. While the lighting landscape evolves, the core principles of the indoor standard continue to guide how we illuminate offices, healthcare facilities, retail spaces, and schools.

The focus remains on creating environments that enhance visual performance while protecting the health of the occupants. The primary focus areas of the standard include:

- Maintained Illuminance: Ensuring that spaces remain properly lit throughout a building’s lifecycle by accounting for equipment ageing and usage patterns.

- Quality of Light: Managing glare, flicker, and stroboscopic effects to reduce eye strain and fatigue.

- Intelligent Controls: The critical role of dynamic lighting solutions that adapt to daylight and occupancy.

- Task Flexibility: Prioritising lighting that can be adjusted to suit various tasks and individual user preferences.

New for 2024: Expanding to Outdoor Workplaces (EN 12464-2)

In 2024, the scope of professional lighting design expanded with the update of the sister standard: EN 12464-2:2024 – Lighting of Workplaces, Part 2: Outdoor Workplaces.

Modern building design no longer treats the interior and exterior as separate entities. This updated standard covers various outdoor working areas—many of which are adjacent to buildings and must be designed in conjunction with indoor spaces. Whether it is a logistics hub, a campus walkway, or a loading zone, the standard ensures that the transition between indoor and outdoor environments is safe, secure, and visually consistent.

Partnering for Smarter Buildings

At EVIO, we work with Helvar, a global leader in lighting control and automation solutions, to bring these cutting-edge technologies to our projects. By combining EVIO’s local expertise with Helvar’s world-class innovation, we deliver flexible, future-proof lighting systems that meet both regulatory requirements and evolving user expectations.

The Helvar Rules of Right Light

While the EN standards provide the necessary regulatory framework, achieving truly “human-centric” lighting requires a deeper level of design expertise. To bridge the gap between compliance and wellbeing, Helvar has developed the Rules of Right Light.

This framework helps specifiers and designers go beyond the minimum requirements. It provides a roadmap for creating lighting that supports the biological and emotional needs of people—balancing energy efficiency with the “right” light at the “right” time and in the “right” place.

Access the Complete Expert Guide

To help you navigate these updates and apply them to your next project, Helvar has released an updated version of their comprehensive whitepaper. This document serves as an essential guide to the latest EN 12464 updates, covering both indoor and outdoor environments, and provides a detailed look at the Rules of Right Light.

title: The Endless Possibilities of Using IoT for Industrial & Commercial Electrical Ecosystem’s Predictive Maintenance.
excerpt: The internet of things (IoT) as we already know, is a giant network of connected things and people. This seemingly endless web of interconnected devices is said to be the pinnacle of technological…
content:
Industry Brief

The internet of things (IoT) as we already know, is a giant network of connected things and people. This seemingly endless web of interconnected devices is said to be the pinnacle of technological advancement. From ordering an Uber to efficient elevator alignment to maximizing energy efficiency, there is literally no limit to the potential physical accomplishments of the IoT. The interesting fact is, we are still around the peripheries of the full accomplishment of the IoT. Of all the fields in which the Internet of Things is set to disrupt norms, the field of electricity is perhaps the most impacted thus far. General Electric (GE) predicts that $1.3 trillion of value can be captured in the electricity value chain from 2016 to 2025 globally by IoT.

Since the discovery of electricity in the 1800s, there has been a global utilization to this energy source. In India alone 414.10 GWh of electricity were used in 2019. Industrial consumption represents 41.6% of this total electricity consumption.

Electrical energy powers almost everything in Industrial buildings, from water pumps to the entire production plant. As much as Industrial facilities rely on electricity for their daily operations, electrical energy comes with a serious caveat – Maintenance.

Electrical maintenance in Industrial facilities can be split into two major areas – Maintenance of energy generating equipment and maintenance of energy consuming devices.

Energy generating equipment or devices refers to those components which are used to manage and generate the electrical energy needs of an Industrial facility. A typical example will be a transformer. Transformers collect electrical energy from the grid and supply to the entire industrial facility. If a transformer were to get bad, the electricity supply in an Industrial facilities will be interrupted, if only momentarily at best. Another example of an energy generating equipment typical to industrial properties is the captive diesel generator.

All electricity generating equipment have life spans and limitations with respect to power input and output, as well as other environmental constraints. These limitations necessitate maintenance.

Energy consuming devices on the other hand are also commonly referred to as end devices. These are the equipment and devices responsible for electricity consumption in Industrial & Commercial facilities. They are found everywhere within the facilities, and are responsible for the day to day operations of industrial and commercial facilities. They include electric kettles, bulbs, conveyor belt, motors, pumps etc. They enhance occupants experience and contribute to the establishment with a competitive edge. Just like electrical energy generating equipment, the end user devices are also a constraint, hence the need for electrical maintenance.

Electrical maintenance covers all aspects of testing, monitoring, fixing and replacing elements of an electrical system. Though the possibilities of using IoT for electrical maintenance are endless, these possibilities will be looked at in line with the four major areas of electrical maintenance – Testing, Monitoring, Fixing and Replacing electrical systems.

How IoT can be used for Electrical Maintenance in Industrial Facilities

- Testing of electrical equipment

Testing of electrical equipment is important not only for the equipment being tested, but is also directly linked to the safety of all the occupants in an Industrial or commercial building. Industrial facilities electrical equipment have to be tested on a regular basis to ensure that the equipment’s are functioning properly and are in line with regulatory standards.

Before the advent of IoT, all forms of electrical appliance testing in industrial & commercial buildings was done manually, based on a schedule. The testing in itself followed standard procedures, such as shaking, smelling and running of the equipment to check for possible faults. The main problem with this form of testing was its heavy reliance on the principle of “If checked parts are OK, then the whole is OK”. This principle was not very effective, because it did not take in to consideration all the components of the Industrial facilities electrical appliance being tested, neither did it evaluate the impact of external environmental factors on the appliance.

With the implementation of IoT systems by Industrial & commercial facilities, this phase of electrical maintenance can be accomplished more effectively. This is achieved by linking up all the Industrial facility’s electrical equipment to the facilities IoT platform, into which analytics are incorporated. Based on the communication between the building’s electrical equipment and every other appliance in the facility, O&M teams will be able to act more efficiently. Leveraging IoT, thresholds could be set within which the system will automatically signal for management to ensure testing or repair. This increases efficiency, as management will not have to schedule for checks when they are not needed, while only getting results based on partial human analytics.

- Monitoring of Electrical Equipment

The monitoring of Industrial facilities electrical equipment implies a continuous and ongoing survey and collection of data with respect to the operations and functionality of the installed electrical system. The crucial nature of this task requires the provision of specific and accurate values on which management can forecast and plan. If these data are collected through human survey, there will always be a margin for error, which could cause management to make all the wrong decisions.

By leveraging the IoT platform, the management of facilities could have real time updates and accurate figures with regards to the performance of electrical equipment within a facility. With the monitoring of the Industrial facilities electrical equipment being done automatically and on a continuous bases, management can be furnished at any time with actual and concrete data on the performance of the different electrical appliance within the facility.

This data could further be accumulated along stated parameters to provide reports and projections with respect to the overall electrical needs of the facility. With IoT incorporation into electrical equipment, everyday electrical equipment transcend from stationary objects to smart devices which can influence the overall electrical maintenance pattern of the installed electrical ecosystem. IoT provides an assurance of constant monitoring and precise data collection for effective decision making.

Today businesses apply three techniques to achieve Peak Overall Equipment Efficiency (OEE) & Utilization to realize their IRR & ROI

- Fixing and replacing electrical equipment

This is the most commonly implemented phase of electrical maintenance. All electrical equipment, no matter how durable, are subject to breakdown. Breakdowns though inherent, if managed properly will not hinder the normal operations of a facility. Unfortunately, it is near impossible to properly manage electrical appliance breakdown relying on a 100% manual system. This is why IoT is the best possible method by which to manage electrical appliance breakdown and replacement.

By using IoT, Industrial facility operators are able to know beforehand (Predictive intelligence) whether or not electrical equipment will breakdown, and when specific electrical equipment will need replacing (Predictive Maintenance).

When electrical equipment in an Industrial facility are interconnected with other devices and linked up with an IoT platform with analytics, the sensors within the electrical equipment pick up valuable and time sensitive data which the human eye could miss. By correlating this data with that from other sensors within the installed electrical ecosystem, as well as liaising with external data sources such as those about the weather, Industrial facility managers can know with near certainty, the best time to inspect the electrical ecosystem, or schedule for repair, servicing or replacement.

Everything can therefore be planned carefully to avoid a breakdown in daily operations.

Conclusion

In conclusion, IoT is being used by various industries, sectors and for increased efficiency and maintenance. Electricity, being the major source of power in almost all sectors is using IoT to manage and maintain equipment and devices that both generate or receive electricity. Some of the most common uses of IoT in electrical maintenance are testing, monitoring and fixing and replacement of electrical equipment.

Below is a snap shot of the solutions and benefits which evio things electrical ecosystem IOT brings to the table. As more and more industry sectors are adopting IoT for electrical maintenance, it is important that you take a look at your facilities and ensure that you are adopting this latest technology in order to gain benefits as well as stay ahead of the curve.

content:

Renovation Overview

The Leela Palace underwent thorough renovation from 2018 to 2021.

Originally built in the colonial era, the hotel now stands as a visually stunning and elegant structure.

Quality, soul, and attention-to-detail were cornerstones of the renovation process.

Lighting Control System

The lighting in all main ‘front of house’ areas is controlled by a Helvar lighting control system.

Evio’s system design ensures perfectly balanced lighting levels in areas such as entrance lobbies, reception, main restaurants, corridors, ballroom, and meeting rooms.

The design aims to cater to the needs of guests and staff while maximizing energy efficiency.

Despite the vast space of Leela Palace and numerous lighting circuits, Evio’s design effectively manages the control system throughout.

The proposed system allows for automatic or manual selection of various lighting scenes at different times of the day.

Each scene is pre-programmed to suit the varying uses of each space and takes daylight contribution into account.

For instance, Diya – Speciality Indian Restaurant features four main lighting scenes programmed for breakfast, lunch, high-tea, and dinner.

Staff can override these scenes via control panels to adjust light levels as needed.

Custom DIN Rail arrangements with dimming and analogue modules were designed and procured by Evio.

User-Friendly System Design

Evio designed the system with a focus on ease of use, allowing hotel staff to create the right ambiance for guests’ well-being.

With meticulous attention to detail, innovative design, and seamless integration, Evio has enhanced the guest experience while ensuring energy efficiency and ease of operation for hotel staff. This project exemplifies Evio’s commitment to excellence in every aspect.
